nameStory: Spearmint gets its name from its distinctive pointed, spear-shaped flower spikes that rise above the plant like tiny green spears. The 'mint' part comes from the Latin 'mentha,' named after a Greek nymph who was transformed into this fragrant plant. You might also hear it called garden mint or common mint since it's the most familiar mint in gardens and kitchens.
description: Spearmint is a spreading perennial herb that grows 1-3 feet tall with square stems and aromatic, toothed leaves. It produces slender spikes of tiny white to pale purple flowers that smell wonderfully fresh and minty when crushed. Originally from Europe and Asia, this escaped garden plant now grows wild throughout New England. It spreads aggressively by underground runners, often forming large patches in moist areas.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to lance-shaped leaves with sharp teeth along the edges, arranged in opposite pairs. Crush a leaf between your fingers - it releases that classic spearmint scent that's sweet and cooling, not harsh like peppermint.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white to pale purple flowers clustered in slender, pointed spikes at the stem tips. The spikes look like miniature bottle brushes and bloom from bottom to top over several weeks.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms spreading colonies through underground runners. Stems are distinctly square when rolled between your fingers - a hallmark of the mint family.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are nearly hairless and have a slightly wrinkled texture with prominent veins. They feel smooth and somewhat thick, not papery thin.

habitat: Look for spearmint in moist, rich soils near streams, ditches, and wet meadows throughout New England. It thrives in partially shaded areas and often escapes from gardens to naturalize in disturbed soils. You'll frequently find it growing alongside other moisture-loving plants like jewelweed and wild bergamot.

seasonality.spring: Fresh green shoots emerge early, with new leaves unfurling and releasing their minty fragrance when brushed against.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time with characteristic flower spikes appearing from July through August. Leaves are at their most aromatic.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and leaves may yellow, but the mint scent remains strong until frost kills back the above-ground portions.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely above ground, but underground runners survive to sprout new colonies in spring.

funFact: Spearmint contains almost no menthol - the compound that gives peppermint its intense cooling sensation - which is why spearmint tastes sweet and mild while peppermint can literally make your eyes water!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with peppermint, but spearmint has a much milder, sweeter scent without the harsh cooling sensation. Remember: spearmint is 'sweet mint' - if crushing a leaf makes your sinuses tingle intensely, you've found peppermint instead.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'garden mint' and 'common mint,' spearmint is actually not native to North America but has become so widespread that many people assume it's always been here. It's the mint most commonly used in cooking and teas.
compareHints: Spearmint differs from other New England mints by its nearly hairless leaves and sweet, mild fragrance. Canada mint has much hairier leaves and grows in wetter areas, while corn mint has a stronger, more medicinal smell. Spearmint's flower spikes are also more distinctly pointed and spear-like than its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Canada mint differs from its relatives by having flowers clustered in the leaf joints rather than in terminal spikes like spearmint, and it's strictly a wetland plant while corn mint tolerates drier soils.
Unlike spearmint and peppermint which form terminal flower spikes, corn mint's flowers cluster in whorls around the stem at leaf joints.
Among New England's mints, apple mint stands out immediately for its fuzzy, rounded leaves that feel like velvet.
Unlike Canada mint which prefers moist but not waterlogged soils, watermint truly loves having wet feet and grows right at the water's edge.
Horse mint differs from our common native Canada mint by being much taller and having woolly-white stems rather than smooth ones.
